**(i) Nitrogen fixation vs lightning**
• **Nitrogen fixation** is the process that changes inert N₂ gas into compounds like ammonia (NH₃) that plants can use; it is essential for the nitrogen cycle.
• **Biological fixation** is carried out by certain bacteria (e.g., Rhizobium, Azotobacter) that possess the enzyme nitrogenase, allowing them to convert N₂ to NH₃ at moderate temperatures.
• **Lightning fixation** occurs when a lightning strike creates extremely high temperatures (≈30,000 °C), breaking the N≡N bond and forming nitrogen oxides (NO, NO₂) that later dissolve in rain to become nitrates.
• Although both processes produce “fixed” nitrogen, they differ in the agent (living microbes vs. electrical discharge), energy source, and ecological role; lightning adds nitrogen directly to soils, while biological fixation often occurs in symbiosis with plants.

• Scientific surveys of human fecal samples have never reported Rhizobium as a resident species, indicating it does not colonize the gut.

question: Explain in full detail, using electron configuration and ionisation enthalpy trends, why sodium is more reactive than magnesium.
after:
**(i) Reactivity Explanation**
• Sodium’s outer electron resides in the **3s** orbital (**[Ne] 3s¹**). This single s‑electron is shielded by the full inner shells, making it relatively far from the nucleus and loosely held, so it is removed with comparatively little energy.
• Magnesium has two electrons in the same **3s** subshell (**[Ne] 3s²**). To achieve a noble‑gas configuration it must lose both electrons, and the removal of the second electron experiences a much stronger effective nuclear charge, raising the ionisation energy.
• The measured **first ionisation enthalpy** of Na (~496 kJ mol⁻¹) is significantly lower than that of Mg (~738 kJ mol⁻¹). This trend follows the periodic pattern where group‑1 elements have lower ionisation energies than the adjacent group‑2 elements.
• Lower ionisation enthalpy means Na atoms can form **Na⁺** ions more readily in reactions such as with water, releasing heat and hydrogen gas, whereas Mg requires more energy to form **Mg²⁺**, slowing its reaction rate.
• Consequently, the combination of a single‑electron configuration and a smaller ionisation enthalpy makes sodium chemically more active than magnesium under similar conditions.

question: Derive the mirror formula and calculate the focal length of the image formed by a plane mirror using the lens-maker equation.
after:
**(i) Derivation of Mirror Formula**
• Draw a principal axis, locate the centre of curvature C, pole P, object point O at distance u from P, and image point I at distance v from P. The incident ray from O strikes the mirror at point Q and reflects through I.
• In triangle CQP, using the small‑angle approximation (\(\sin \theta \approx \tan \theta \approx \theta\)), we obtain \(\frac{CQ}{CP} = \frac{OQ}{OP} = \frac{u}{R}\) and similarly \(\frac{CQ}{CP} = \frac{IQ}{IP} = \frac{v}{R}\).
• Equating the two expressions for \(\frac{CQ}{CP}\) gives \(\frac{u}{R} = \frac{v}{R}\) → \(\frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v} = \frac{2}{R}\). Re‑arranging, the focal length f is defined as \(f = \frac{R}{2}\), leading to the mirror formula \(\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v}\).

**(ii) Focal Length of a Plane Mirror**
• A plane mirror is a special case of a spherical mirror where the reflecting surface is flat; geometrically this corresponds to a radius of curvature R that is infinitely large (R → ∞).

Pluto is not classified as a planet; there are only eight planets in the solar system.
**(i) List of planets**
• Mercury – the innermost planet, it has a very thin atmosphere and extreme temperature variations.

• Earth – the only known planet to support life, with liquid water and a protective **ozone layer**.

• Jupiter – the largest planet, a gas giant with a massive **magnetic field** and many moons.
• Saturn – famous for its extensive **ring system** composed of ice and rock particles.
• Uranus – an ice giant that rotates on its side, giving it extreme seasonal variations.
• Neptune – the farthest recognized planet, known for its strong **winds** and blue color due to methane.

**(ii) Why Pluto is not the smallest planet**
• Pluto is designated a **dwarf planet** because it shares its orbital zone with other objects in the Kuiper Belt, meaning it has not cleared its neighbourhood.
• This classification, made by the IAU in 2006, excludes Pluto from the list of planets, so it cannot be called the smallest planet.
• Consequently, all eight recognized planets are larger than Pluto, making Pluto the smallest known dwarf planet in the solar system.

**(i) Atomic Number**
• Indium (symbol **In**) is a post‑transition metal placed in **group 13** of the periodic table, indicating it has three electrons in its outer shell.
• Its **atomic number is 49**, meaning each indium atom contains 49 protons in the nucleus.
• It belongs to the **fifth period**, so its electrons occupy the fifth energy level.
• In the Class 8 curriculum, indium is described as a soft, silvery‑white metal with a low melting point and good ductility.

**(ii) Common Compounds**
• **Indium oxide (In₂O₃)** – formed when indium reacts with oxygen at high temperature; it appears as a white solid and conducts electricity, making it useful in transparent conductive coatings for touch‑screens.
• This oxide is also employed in solar‑cell technology because of its ability to allow light to pass while conducting charge.
• **Indium chloride (InCl₃)** – obtained by reacting indium metal with hydrochloric acid; it crystallises as a colour‑less solid.
• It serves as a precursor for preparing other indium salts and is used in semiconductor manufacturing for doping processes.
Indium (In) has atomic number 49, and two common compounds are indium oxide (In₂O₃) and indium chloride (InCl₃).
